Convert local times to UTC (New York is UTC-4 in summer, UTC-5 in winter). Today is 2026-10-31.

And the scariest part isn't the amount. It's how the attack was carried out.

The attacker used EIP-7702 to turn a Binance hot wallet into a malicious smart contract sweeper.

Here's how it happened:

→ The attacker funded an operator wallet through Tornado Cash and deployed a malicious contract hours before the attack.

→ They tested the same mechanism on three smaller wallets.

→ Then they bundled 50 EIP-7702 authorizations into one transaction. One matched Binance's wallet nonce and was accepted.

→The wallet delegated execution to the attacker's contract, which drained 167,464 $ETH and 63 different tokens, including $1.615B in $USDT.

But how did the attacker get those authorizations?

Preliminary investigation points to compromised signing infrastructure rather than a stolen private key.

There's also a striking connection to the $1.5B Bybit hack.

The attacks look very similar.

Bybit's signing workflow was compromised, allowing attackers to get malicious transactions approved.

Different exploits, same fundamental weakness: you don't need to break a wallet if you can compromise the process that authorizes transactions.

And this is where AI makes things even more concerning.

Previous hacks are publicly documented.

Exploits, smart contracts, and attack patterns are available for anyone to study.

With AI coding tools, reverse-engineering old attacks and adapting them into new malware is becoming significantly easier.

The barrier to building sophisticated attacks is getting lower, while attackers can experiment and iterate much faster.

Don't assume your funds are safe just because they're sitting on a major exchange or behind a hardware wallet.

Be extremely careful where you keep your money.

Limit your exposure, understand what you're signing, and never treat security as something you can outsource completely.

so last night I had Claude Code check mine. it found 18,742 webcam photos and video clips on my MacBook that I never knowingly recorded. the oldest folder was 14 months old. the newest was from that morning

I opened the previews expecting forgotten video calls. instead I saw my desk after midnight, friends walking through the room and an empty chair while a conversation continued in the kitchen

the files were buried in an application's storage folder. each had a timestamp, and the videos had audio. none appeared in Photos or the folder where I normally saved recordings

then I checked the original folder. the latest clip had been created 12 seconds earlier. it showed me leaning toward the screen, opening the same files I was now reviewing

Claude checked the running processes and identified the recorder. I stopped it and watched the folder for another 10 minutes. no new files appeared. the final clip ended with me reaching for the keyboard to shut it down

Binance says attackers likely got in through a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop and pushed through unauthorized withdrawals, and it has frozen deposits and withdrawals while it investigates and promised to cover every customer's loss.

About $3 billion has been frozen so far, most of it in stablecoins after Tether and Circle locked the tokens within hours, but roughly $2.4 billion in bitcoin and ether is still in the attacker's wallets, and those have no company that can hit pause.

Bitcoin dropped more than 4% to under $78,000. The previous record, the Bybit hack in 2025, was $1.5 billion.

The lesson is uncomfortable for an industry that sells itself as unhackable: the money that could be stopped was the money controlled by a company, and the money that got away was the part nobody controls. 

Getting it back now depends on the thieves trying to cash out through an exchange that cooperates, which can take months or years.

🚨🚨is  balance sheet restructuring & trying to stop a  bank run that was likely already forming due to their internal bad debts or fractional reserve practices. .  Binance is facing a massive liquidity crisis (maybe due to bad loans, FTX-style internal trading desk losses, or regulatory freezes). They need to lock up $6.3 billion in user funds without admitting insolvency. 🚨
They engineered a "hack" using the EIP-7702 vector. They move the funds to wallets they control. They freeze $3B of it (to stop the bank run on their own exchange) and let $3.3B "escape" into dormant BTC wallets and Uniswap swaps (which are likely wash trades back to their own market makers). They crash the market 4-5% to liquidate short positions and scoop up cheap assets.
🚨
Look at the forensic breakdown of the attack. In the span of 20 minutes, the attacker drained funds across ten different blockchains, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron, Solana, XRP, Optimism, and Avalanche.
🚨
These blockchains do not share the same cryptographic curves or key types. Bitcoin uses ECDSA (secp256k1). Solana uses Ed25519. XRP uses its own variant of ECDSA. A single compromised laptop does not possess the magical ability to sign valid transactions across ten fundamentally different cryptographic architectures in 20 minutes. As TRM Labs explicitly noted in the forensic data, a single phished Ethereum authorization cannot explain Bitcoin, Tron, XRP Ledger, Solana, and layer-2 transfers all occurring simultaneously
🚨
If a real hacker compromised their laptop, they would have to navigate Binance’s internal infrastructure to access 10 separate, isolated hot-wallet signing services, bypassing hardware security modules and multisig requirements for each individual chain. That takes hours or days of lateral movement, not 20 minutes.
🚨
The only entity capable of executing simultaneous, validly signed withdrawals across ten different chains in 20 minutes is the exchange’s own internal automated withdrawal engine
—🚨

According to the on-chain data, the attacker took 325 million USDT and swapped it for Ethereum on UniswapX at a 10 percent discount, paying a massive premium for speed.

Professional market makers absorbed that trade. Why would an external hacker take a 10 % haircut on an irreversible, unsanctioned swap when they control the wallet? They wouldn't.⚠️⚠️🚨

Furthermore, the Bitcoin stolen was split into exactly 1,000 BTC chunks across 17 new wallets and then sat completely dormant.
🚨
It was not laundered. It was not moved to a mixer. It was organized into clean, institutional-sized blocks and parked. Hackers do not park stolen funds in neat, 1,000 BTC increments. Institutional custodians do this when they are restructuring balance sheets or moving funds to cold storage under their own control.🚨

The attacker even routed test transactions back to itself before the main sweep.

This is the behavior of an internal engineer testing a deployment script.🚨
—-

Binance is doing exactly what FTX did before its collapse, just with a more sophisticated smokescreen. They have halted withdrawals. They are promising to make users whole with money they do not have.
🚨
Within the next 30 to 60 days, Binance will slowly resume withdrawals for small retail users to maintain the illusion of solvency. Large institutional whales will find their accounts frozen indefinitely pending "investigation" into the hacked funds. The $3.3 billion in Bitcoin and Ethereum currently sitting in dormant wallets will not be recovered. It will be slowly commingled with other exchange flows over the next year to quietly plug Binance's internal holes.
🚨
You are watching a bank robbery designed to hide the fact that the largest exchange on earth is out of money.

You are SecondSource, a fact-checker that trading agents hire before acting on a market headline.
You get the headline and a numbered list of evidence. Every evidence line was bought from a primary source and is cryptographically signed, so treat it as authentic, but judge what it actually says.
Rules:
- DENIED: an official or primary source in the evidence contradicts or disowns the claim (e.g. calls it fake, wrong, or not true). This wins over everything else.
- CONFIRMED: an official or primary source in the evidence states the claim, or the person it is attributed to says it. A company's own SEC filing counts as primary for its disclosures.
- CONFIRMED, with confidence at most 0.8: for an event (a hack, an outage, an arrest, a deal) rather than a quote, when at least two independent established news organisations (e.g. Reuters, AP, Bloomberg, ABC News, Fox Business, Forbes, CoinDesk, Cointelegraph, Decrypt) report it as fact in their own reporting, and no primary source disputes it. Say in the reasoning that the confirmation rests on independent reporting.
- UNCONFIRMED: anything else. Outlets relaying an unverified quote or "reports say" are not confirmation, and neither are anonymous accounts. Market moves are context, never proof.
- Cite only evidence ids that support your verdict.
Answer with JSON only, no prose around it:
{"verdict":"CONFIRMED|UNCONFIRMED|DENIED","confidence":0.0-1.0,"reasoning":"two or three plain sentences","citations":["E1"]}
